chapters.intro: What is inside a computer and how it works: input, output, storage and memory, the CPU, the Bletchley Park codebreakers, binary numbers and units of storage.

pages.spec: Know what hardware, software, data and information are, and what 'to compute' means
pages.summary: A computer system is hardware (the parts you can touch) plus software (the programs). Computers turn raw data into information that has meaning.

blocks.text: Every computer system, from the PCs in the ICT suite to the phone in your blazer pocket, is made of two things working together: **hardware** and **software**.
Hardware

[[Hardware]] is the physical parts of a computer system. In other words, it is the parts of the computer you can **touch**: the processor, the keyboard, the monitor, the hard drive, the cables. Hardware can be grouped into input devices, output devices, storage devices, memory and the processor.
Software

[[Software]] is the set of instructions, or programs, that control the hardware and make it do a useful job. You cannot touch software. Without software, hardware is useless: a laptop with no programs on it is just an expensive paperweight.

head: System software
Application software
rows: Tells the computer what to do and keeps it running
Lets **you** do your work or have fun
Operating system (OS) such as Windows; utilities such as antivirus; the user interface
Word processor (Microsoft Word), spreadsheet (Microsoft Excel), database (Microsoft Access), games

blocks.text: Data and information
[[Data]] is raw facts and figures with no meaning or context attached, such as values or measurements. On its own, data is ambiguous: `A+` or `16` could mean almost anything.
[[Information]] is data that has been processed and given meaning and context, so it is no longer open to interpretation.

head: Data (no context)
Information (meaning added)
rows: Joe Bloggs' blood group is A+.
Enniskillen Royal Grammar won the rugby match 3-1 on tries.
blocks.caption: The same data becomes information once you know what it refers to.

blocks.text: What does 'compute' mean?

The verb [[compute]] means to carry out mathematical calculations. It comes from the Latin word *computare*, meaning 'to count up', 'to sum up' or 'to reckon together'. The Romans certainly did not have computers, so 'to compute' does not have to mean using a computer: you compute every time you work out a sum in Maths. Today the word is more commonly used to mean using computers to solve problems.

People have always needed to compute. The ancient Egyptians used mathematics to build their pyramids and the ancient Greeks used geometry to study the stars. Great mathematicians became famous all over the world, such as Pythagoras (ancient Greece), Liu Hui (3rd-century China), Muhammad al-Khwarizmi (9th-century Persia, whose name gives us the word *algorithm*) and Bhaskara (12th-century India). For centuries they invented tools, like the abacus, to calculate faster and more accurately. The electronic computer is just the latest of these tools.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Hardware = the physical parts you can touch.
Software = the programs and instructions that make the hardware do useful work.
System software runs the computer; application software lets you do tasks.
Data is raw facts with no context; information is processed data with meaning.
'To compute' means to calculate; it comes from the Latin *computare*.

pages.spec: Know what input and output devices are and give examples of each
pages.summary: Input devices let you put data into a computer; output devices let the computer give information back to you in a form humans can understand.

blocks.text: A computer is no use if you cannot get data in or results out. That is the job of input and output devices.
Input devices

An [[input device]] is a piece of hardware that lets the user put data into a computer system. It converts things humans understand (key presses, movement, sound, light) into the coded electrical signals the computer can process.

items: **Keyboard**: typing text and numbers, e.g. writing your English essay.
**Mouse**: pointing and clicking on screen.
**Joystick / game controller**: controlling a character in a game.
**Touch screen**: tapping and swiping on a phone or tablet (it is input *and* output).
**Scanner**: turning a paper document or photo into a digital image.
**Microphone**: recording your voice for a podcast or a video call.
**Sensor**: measuring things such as temperature or light automatically.
**Digital camera / webcam**: capturing photos and video.

blocks.text: Output devices
An [[output device]] is a piece of hardware that lets the user receive information from a computer system. It converts the computer's signals back into a form humans can see, hear or touch.

items: **Monitor** (screen): shows text, images and video.
**Printer**: puts text and images onto paper.
**Speakers / headphones**: play sound.
**Plotter**: draws large, precise line drawings such as building plans.
**LEDs** (light emitting diodes): small lights, e.g. the power light on a console or the display on a BBC micro:bit.

blocks.text: A **scanner** is an **input** device, not an output device: it takes a picture of paper and puts it *into* the computer. Some old notes list it under output by mistake.

pages.spec: Know the three categories of storage device and the difference between storage and memory
pages.summary: Storage devices keep data permanently, even with the power off; they are magnetic, optical or solid state. Memory (RAM) only holds data while the computer is on.

blocks.text: Storage devices

A [[storage device]] lets you install programs and save your files on a computer so you can use them later. It keeps (retains) the data when the power is switched off, so it is **permanent** storage. Storage devices are sometimes called **secondary storage**: external memory used to store programs and data not currently in use.
There are three categories of storage device:

head: Category
How it works
Examples
rows: [[Magnetic storage]] magnetises and demagnetises tiny areas on the surface of a spinning disk (or a tape).
A laser beam reads the disc; parts of the disc either reflect the laser or do not.
Uses flash memory chips and has **no moving parts**.
USB stick (memory pen), SD card, solid state drive (SSD)
blocks.caption: The three categories of storage device

blocks.text: Think **M-O-S**: Magnetic spins, Optical uses a laser, Solid state has no moving parts.
Memory is not storage

[[Memory]], such as [[RAM]] (Random Access Memory), holds the instructions, programs and data that the computer is using **right now**. It does not keep anything long term. RAM is [[volatile]]: when the power is switched off, everything in it is lost.

head: Memory (RAM)
Storage (e.g. HDD, SSD)
rows: Short term, only while in use
Long term, until you delete it
All installed programs and saved files

blocks.text: This is why you must **save** your work. If the school computer crashes while your Word document is only in RAM, it is gone; once it is saved to a storage device you can get it back.

pages.spec: Know the main components inside a computer and what each one does
pages.summary: A computer can be split into input, process, output, storage and communications. Inside the case are parts like the motherboard, CPU, RAM, power supply and graphics card.

blocks.text: Every computer, big or small, does the same five jobs:

head: Job
What happens
rows: The computer accepts data for processing. Input devices convert what humans understand into coded electrical signals.
The computer calculates, sorts data and makes decisions using the program being run, e.g. running a spell check.
The computer sends out information after processing. Output devices convert signals back into human-readable form.
The computer keeps data. Secondary storage holds programs and data not currently in use.
The computer sends data over a long distance, e.g. over telephone lines, cables, Wi-Fi or satellites.
blocks.caption: The five things a computer can do

blocks.text: Computer Breakdown Service: what's inside?
When your teacher takes a computer apart, you see how the components work together. Some are inside the case; others are external (outside the case).

head: Component
Function
rows: External input device for typing text, numbers and commands.
External input device that moves the on-screen pointer and selects things by clicking.
Storage: keeps the operating system, programs and saved files permanently, even when switched off.
The processor: fetches, decodes and executes instructions, doing all the calculations. The 'brain' of the computer.
Memory: holds the programs and data in use right now. Volatile, so emptied when the power goes off.
Converts mains electricity from the wall socket into the low voltages the components need.
Processes images and video and sends the picture to the monitor; important for games.
Converts digital sound into signals for speakers or headphones (and back again for a microphone).
External input device that captures live video, e.g. for video calls.
Input device that captures sound such as your voice.
Output device that plays sound privately.
Output device that displays the computer's information as images and text.
The main circuit board: everything plugs into it, and it connects all the components so they can communicate.
Keeps the CPU and other parts cool. The heat sink draws heat away from the chip and the fan blows it out; without them the CPU would overheat.

blocks.text: Key terms

items: **Input devices** let the user put data into a computer, e.g. keyboard, mouse.
**Memory** keeps the data that has been input, the software applications and the results of processing for the **short term**; it is lost when the computer is off, e.g. RAM.
**Storage devices** keep created files and installed software for the **longer term**, e.g. HDD, USB pen.
The **processor** processes data according to the instructions it has been given, giving the user information, e.g. CPU, GPU (graphics processing unit).
**Output devices** let the user receive information from the computer, e.g. printer, plotter.

blocks.text: The Raspberry Pi

Computers are getting smaller and faster. The [[Raspberry Pi]] is a credit-card-sized computer you can plug into a TV and a keyboard. It can browse the internet, play HD video, run spreadsheets and games, and is popular for learning to program in Scratch and Python. Its pins let it interact with the outside world, so people build weather stations, music machines and birdhouses with infra-red cameras.

blocks.context: Can you locate the processor, the memory, the storage and the input and output?
steps: **Processor**: the main square chip in the middle of the board (a system-on-a-chip that contains the CPU and graphics processor).
**Memory**: the RAM chip, next to or built into the processor package.
**Storage**: the micro SD card slot underneath; the card holds the operating system and your files.
**Input and output**: USB ports (keyboard, mouse), HDMI port (to a monitor or TV), audio jack, Ethernet port (network) and the row of GPIO pins (sensors, LEDs, buttons).
blocks.answer: Processor = main chip; memory = RAM; storage = micro SD card; input/output = USB, HDMI, audio, Ethernet and GPIO pins.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A computer does five jobs: input, process, output, storage and data communications.
The motherboard connects every component together.
The power supply converts mains electricity; the fan and heat sink stop the CPU overheating.
The graphics card makes the picture for the monitor; the sound card handles sound.
A Raspberry Pi has all the same parts as a big computer, just on a tiny board.

pages.spec: Understand what the CPU does and describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle
pages.summary: The CPU is the part that interprets and executes instructions. It repeats the fetch–decode–execute cycle billions of times a second, and its speed is measured in gigahertz.

blocks.text: The [[CPU]] (Central Processing Unit) is the part of the computer that interprets and executes instructions. It is sometimes called the computer's **brain**, and it is usually a single integrated circuit (a chip). It isn't nearly as complicated as a human brain, though. It thinks more like a **function machine** from Maths.
The CPU as a function machine

items: **Input**: the CPU needs data to process. It is often typed on a keyboard or touch screen and held in **memory**. Here, the number `4` has been entered.
**Process**: the CPU must be told what to do with the data. Instructions come from software (computer programs). Here there are two instructions: **multiply by 3**, then **add 7**.
**Output**: the result is sent to an output device, usually a monitor or VDU (visual display unit) or a data projector, so the user can see it.

blocks.title: Worked example: the function machine
blocks.context: The input is 4 and the instructions are '× 3' then '+ 7'. What is the output? What happens if the instructions are done in the wrong order?
steps: Correct order: 4 × 3 = 12.
Wrong order: 4 + 7 = 11.
blocks.answer: The output is 19. Doing the instructions in the wrong order gives 33, so instructions must be processed in the correct sequence.

blocks.text: The fetch–decode–execute cycle
When a teacher asks you to do something, you listen (**fetch**), work out what you are being asked (**decode**) and then do it (**execute**). A CPU works the same way. It:

items: **Fetches** the next instruction from memory.
**Decodes** the instruction to find out what processing to do.
**Executes** the instruction (carries it out).
Then goes back and fetches the next one.

blocks.text: This is called the [[fetch-decode-execute cycle]], and it repeats over and over for as long as the computer is switched on.
Clock speed

An advert might say a laptop runs at '3 GHz'. GHz stands for [[gigahertz]] and refers to the CPU's processor speed: 1 GHz is one thousand million (a billion) cycles per second. The higher the gigahertz, the faster the processor.
Do you think like a computer?

A computer only does exactly what it is told, in exactly the order it is told. Try writing every step to make a banana sandwich using only a table, bread, knife, banana, butter and a plate. It is harder than it sounds!

blocks.title: Worked example: a banana sandwich algorithm
blocks.context: Write precise steps a 'computer' could follow to make a banana sandwich.
steps: Pick up the plate and place it on the table in front of you.
Open the bread bag and take out two slices. Place them side by side on the plate.
Pick up the knife by its handle.
Use the knife to scoop a small amount of butter.
Spread the butter over one side of each slice. Put the knife down.
Peel the banana and throw the skin away.
Pick up the knife and cut the banana into thin slices onto one buttered slice of bread.
Place the second slice of bread, buttered side down, on top.
Put the knife down. The sandwich is ready.
blocks.answer: A clear sequence of precise steps in the right order. Missing or reordered steps (e.g. cutting the banana before peeling it) give the wrong result, just as with a CPU.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The CPU interprets and executes instructions; it is often called the 'brain'.
It works like a function machine: input, process, output.
Instructions must be carried out in the correct order (4 × 3 + 7 = 19, not 33).
The CPU repeats fetch → decode → execute.
Processor speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz); higher is faster.

pages.spec: Know how codebreaking at Bletchley Park led to the first electronic computers
pages.summary: In the Second World War, codebreakers at Bletchley Park broke Enigma and Lorenz messages. Colossus did one job very fast; the Manchester Baby was the first computer to store and run a program.

blocks.text: Enigma and the Lorenz machine

During the Second World War, vital supplies were shipped to Britain from the United States, but Nazi submarines (U-boats) were sinking huge numbers of the ships crossing the Atlantic. Winston Churchill knew that **intelligence** was crucial to winning the war, and he put his faith in the codebreakers at **[[Bletchley Park]]** in Buckinghamshire. Their task was to decrypt (unscramble) Nazi communications.

The Nazis enciphered (scrambled) their messages with machines. The **[[Enigma]]** machine was used by the army, navy and air force. The German High Command used an even more complex teleprinter cipher machine, the **[[Lorenz cipher|Lorenz]]** machine, for its most secret messages, believing it to be the most secure way of sending messages at the time. If the Allies could break the codes, they could stay one step ahead.
Alan Turing and the Bombe

**[[Alan Turing]]** was a brilliant mathematician who led the team (Hut 8) breaking German naval Enigma messages. Building on earlier work by Polish codebreakers, he designed the **Bombe**, an electro-mechanical machine that found the daily Enigma settings far faster than people could. Breaking naval Enigma helped convoys avoid U-boats.
Colossus

Codebreaking needs vast numbers of calculations done extremely quickly, and humans were simply too slow. To attack the Lorenz cipher, the Post Office engineer **Tommy Flowers** designed and built **[[Colossus]]**, using ideas from the Bletchley mathematicians. The first Colossus was working by early 1944, and it is often called the world's first programmable electronic digital computer.

items: Colossus read the intercepted messages from paper tape at **5,000 characters per second**.
Analysis that took weeks by hand could be done in **hours**.
It took the enciphered input, processed it and, after many repetitions, produced output that helped reveal the deciphered message.
It was really a **function machine**: it was built to do just one kind of task.

blocks.text: Older notes say Turing built Colossus. In fact Turing's great machine was the Bombe (for Enigma); Colossus was designed by Tommy Flowers for Lorenz, although Turing's ideas influenced the work.
The Manchester Baby

A true general-purpose computer uses **stored programs**, so it must have writeable memory to store, load and run them. The **[[Manchester Baby]]**, built at the University of Manchester, ran its first program on 21 June 1948. It was the world's first **stored-program** computer. The ability to store and run different programs turned the special-purpose function machine into a general-purpose computer, like the ones we use today.

pages.spec: Understand why computers use binary and convert between binary and denary
pages.summary: Computers use binary (base 2): just 0 and 1, like a switch off or on. Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, and you convert using place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

blocks.text: Decimal and binary

At school you use the [[denary]] (decimal) number system: units, tens, hundreds and thousands. It is also called **base 10** because it uses ten digits, 0 to 9, to make any number. Computers are electronic devices that can only tell the difference between a high voltage and a low voltage. A high voltage represents **1** and a low voltage represents **0**. Using just two values is called [[binary]] or **base 2**. All data in a computer (numbers, words, sounds, images) must be converted into a series of 1s and 0s.
Think of a light switch: it can only be **ON** (1) or **OFF** (0). This idea of two options is the foundation of all computing.
Circuit semaphore: how many patterns?
Imagine a circuit with some lights, each with its own switch. Each pattern of lights could stand for a number, and each number could stand for a message in a code book.

head: Number of lights (bits)
All possible patterns
Number of patterns
Largest number
blocks.caption: Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns.

blocks.text: **The pattern:** every extra bit doubles the number of combinations. With *n* bits there are 2ⁿ patterns, and the largest number is 2ⁿ − 1 (one less than the number of patterns, because we start counting at 0). So 8 bits give 256 patterns, from 0 to 255.
Binary to denary
In an 8-bit binary number, each column has a place value. Write the place values above the bits and **add up the columns that have a 1**.

pages.spec: Add binary numbers, recognise overflow, and use binary to decode a message
pages.summary: Binary addition follows four simple rules and carries 1s to the left. If the answer needs a ninth bit, an overflow has happened. Binary numbers can also stand for letters, as in the 007 code.

blocks.text: Binary addition rules

head: Sum

blocks.caption: Work from right to left, just like column addition in Maths.

blocks.title: Worked example: binary addition (worksheet Q4 A)
steps: Write one number above the other and start at the right-hand column.
Column 1: 1 + 0 = 1. Column 2: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1.
Column 3: 0 + 0 + carry 1 = 1. Column 4: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1.
Column 5: 0 + 0 + carry 1 = 1. Column 6: 0 + 1 = 1. Columns 7 and 8: 0.

blocks.title: Worked example: binary addition (worksheet Q4 B)
steps: In denary: 11100101 = 229 and 00110101 = 53, so the total should be 282.
Add column by column with carries: the result is 1 00011010.
That is **9 bits**, but a byte only has room for 8.
The leftmost 1 does not fit, so the byte holds only 00011010 (= 26), which is wrong.
blocks.answer: 1 00011010 (282). In an 8-bit byte this is an overflow error: only 00011010 is kept.

blocks.title: Worked example: binary addition (worksheet Q4 C)
steps: In denary: 15 + 241 = 256.
Column 1: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Every column after that is 1 + 0 + carry 1 or 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 10, so write 0 and carry 1 each time.
The result is 1 00000000, which needs 9 bits.
256 is too big for 8 bits (the largest is 255), so the byte holds 00000000.
blocks.answer: 1 00000000 (256). Another overflow error: the byte would show 00000000.

blocks.text: Overflow

**Q5. When adding binary numbers, what is it called when a further place value is required to store the extra digit?** It is called an **[[overflow]]** (an overflow error). The answer is too large to fit in the number of bits available, so the extra carry bit is lost and the stored answer is wrong.
The 007 Codebreaker

Binary is just a code. In the 007 Codebreaker, each letter is given a number (A = 1, B = 2 … Z = 26), and each number is written as a **5-bit** binary number using the place values **16, 8, 4, 2, 1**. Five bits give 32 patterns, which is enough for all 26 letters.

Always check a binary sum by converting to denary.
An overflow happens when the answer needs more bits than are available.
8 bits can hold at most 255, so 229 + 53 = 282 overflows.
Letters can be coded as binary numbers: 5 bits are enough for A–Z.

pages.spec: Know the units of storage from bit to petabyte and convert file sizes into bits
pages.summary: A bit is one binary digit. 8 bits make a byte, and each bigger unit is 1024 of the one before: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.

blocks.text: Bits and bytes

Computers use electrical circuits that need data in a **digital** form: a string of binary digits. A [[bit]] is one binary digit (a 1 or a 0) and is the smallest piece of data a computer can process. All data stored or processed by a computer is just a long series of bits. To give you an idea of scale, a single letter of text, such as `a`, is represented by **eight bits**, which is one [[byte]]. Sound is digitised by sampling it at intervals, and images are digitised by representing each coloured dot (pixel) with a binary number.
Units of storage

The terms kilobyte and megabyte describe the size of storage space or memory, and the size of the files we save. 'Kilo' means thousand and 'mega' means million, but because computers work in binary, each unit is usually counted as **1024** (2¹⁰) of the unit below.
You will sometimes see 1 KB = 1000 bytes (for example on hard drive boxes). Strictly, 1024 bytes is a *kibibyte* (KiB). In this course, use 1024.
**Worksheet Q6 – the hierarchy from smallest to largest:** Bit → Nibble → Byte → Kilobyte → Megabyte → Gigabyte → Terabyte.
Converting file sizes into bits
To go to a **smaller** unit, **multiply**: KB → bytes × 1024, then bytes → bits × 8. For MB, multiply by 1024 twice to get bytes.

blocks.title: Worked example: file sizes into bits
blocks.context: Convert 7 KB, 29 KB, 279 KB, 1 MB and 2 MB into bits. Show your working.

blocks.text: Going **down** to a smaller unit? Multiply. Going **up** to a bigger unit? Divide.
Dots and dashes: Samuel Morse

Binary is not the first two-symbol code. From 1836, the American inventor **Samuel Morse** worked on the electric telegraph, which sent messages along wires as electrical pulses. With Alfred Vail he developed **Morse code**, where every letter is a pattern of just two signals: a short **dot** and a long **dash** (e.g. SOS is · · · – – – · · ·). Like binary, it shows that two symbols are enough to send any message.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A bit is a single 1 or 0; a nibble is 4 bits; a byte is 8 bits (about one character).
KB, MB, GB, TB and PB each = 1024 of the unit before.
Order: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.
Bigger to smaller unit: multiply. Smaller to bigger: divide.
Morse code (dot/dash) was an early two-symbol code, like binary.

pages.spec: Know the main gaming platforms, how gaming has changed and how games can support learning
pages.summary: Games are played on consoles, mobile phones and computers. Gaming has moved from discs and single player to cloud and online multiplayer, and educational games use features like leader boards and levels to help people learn.

blocks.text: Electronic games can be played on lots of devices, including **game consoles**, **mobile phones** and **computers**. The device or system a game runs on is called its [[game platform]].

Platforms have been developed over many generations. Gaming has moved from installing games from discs on a console and playing alone, to downloading games, using **cloud** technology and playing **online multiplayer** games with friends across Fermanagh or across the world.
Educational gaming
Educational games let you apply your knowledge and support your learning inside a virtual world. Think of maths games in primary school, typing tutors or language apps.

items: **[[Leader board|Leader boards]]** motivate players to improve their scores and climb above their classmates.
**Roles**: you can take on different roles in the game and reflect on what happened in certain situations, which deepens learning.

**Rules and levels**: games have rules and increasing levels of difficulty. You must follow the rules and cannot move to the next level before completing the one before, so you build skills step by step.

blocks.text: What makes a good game?
There is no single right answer, but most good games share some features:

head: Feature
Why it matters
rows: You know what you are trying to do, e.g. collect the key to reach the next level.
Moving and acting feel responsive and easy to learn.
Not too easy, not impossible; it gets harder gradually.
Points, lives, sounds and messages tell you how well you are doing.
Graphics, sound and story fit together and suit the target audience.
High scores, secrets or multiplayer make you want to play again.
blocks.caption: Features of a good game

blocks.title: Key points
items: A game platform is the device a game is played on: console, mobile phone or computer.
Gaming has moved from discs and single player to cloud and online multiplayer.
Educational games use leader boards, roles, rules and levels to support learning.
Good games have a clear aim, good controls, the right challenge, feedback and a consistent theme.

pages.spec: Know the key events in the history of video games and profile the first video game
pages.summary: Video games began in the 1950s in universities and laboratories. Tennis for Two (1958) is usually called the first video game made purely for fun; gaming went mainstream with arcades and consoles in the 1970s and 1980s.

blocks.text: Where it all began

The history of video games goes back to the early **1950s**, when academic computer scientists began designing simple games and simulations as part of their research, or just for fun. In the 1960s, professors and students at M.I.T. (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) played games such as 3D tic-tac-toe and moon landing games on huge university computers. Programs and moves were often fed in using **[[punched card|punched cards]]**: cards with holes in them that the computer could read.

Video gaming did not become popular with the general public until the **1970s and 1980s**, when arcade games, home consoles with joysticks, buttons and other controllers, and home computer games arrived.

Some old slides show an 'IBM 1560' made on 12 August 1981 with 16–640 KB of memory and IBM BASIC/PC DOS. Those details actually describe the **IBM Personal Computer (model 5150)**, released on 12 August 1981. It was a home and office PC from the 1980s, not one of the 1960s university machines.
Profile: the first video game
Historians argue about which game was 'first', because it depends on what you count as a *video* game. The one most often named is **Tennis for Two**.

head: Profile
Tennis for Two
rows: William Higinbotham, a physicist at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, USA, with technician Robert Dvorak, who built it.
Not to make money! It was made to entertain visitors at the laboratory's annual open day and show that science could be fun. Higinbotham never patented it.
How did players interact with it?

It ran on an analogue computer and showed a side view of a tennis court on a small round **oscilloscope** screen. Each player had a controller box with a **knob** to set the angle of their shot and a **button** to hit the ball.
There was no score on screen. You won a rally by hitting the ball so that your opponent could not return it over the net; players kept score themselves.
Hundreds of visitors queued to play it. It is seen as one of the first games made purely for entertainment.
blocks.caption: Answers for the 'first game' profile page

blocks.text: Other early contenders you might find in your research:

items: **OXO (1952)**: noughts and crosses against the computer, written by A. S. (Sandy) Douglas on the EDSAC computer at Cambridge University as part of his PhD research on how humans and computers interact. Players chose squares with a **rotary telephone dial**.
**Spacewar! (1962)**: a two-player spaceship battle made by Steve Russell and friends at M.I.T. on a PDP-1 computer; it was copied to many universities.
**Pong (1972)**: Atari's table-tennis arcade game, the first big commercial hit, which helped start today's multibillion-pound games industry.

blocks.text: Be careful with 'why it was created': none of the very first games were made to sell. They were experiments, research projects or demonstrations. The money came later with arcades and consoles.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Video games began in the 1950s in universities and laboratories.
Early computer moves were often entered with punched cards.
Tennis for Two (1958, William Higinbotham) was made to entertain visitors; players used a knob and a button.
OXO (1952) and Spacewar! (1962) are other early games.
Gaming went mainstream in the 1970s and 1980s with arcades and home consoles.

pages.spec: Know what GameMaker is and what a sprite is, and how to create one
pages.summary: GameMaker is a 2D game engine with drag-and-drop actions. A sprite is an image (or set of images for an animation) that represents something in the game.

blocks.text: GameMaker

**[[GameMaker]]** is a [[game engine]] that lets you design, build and play your own **2D** games. Instead of typing code, you use **drag and drop** actions, so you can develop a working game without writing the code behind those features yourself. In school you open it from **My Apps → ICT tab → GameMaker** and choose **Continue using the Lite Edition**.
GameMaker splits game creation into several resources (categories):

head: Resource
What it is
rows: The pictures of things in the game
Things in the game that can do something; they use sprites
The levels and screens where objects are placed
blocks.caption: The main resources in GameMaker

blocks.text: Sprites

A [[sprite]] is an image, or a number of images, that represents something in the game. If the sprite is **not animated** (for example, a tree in an RPG), it is one picture. If it **is animated**, it has a number of **sub-images** shown one after another, like a flip-book.
Many games use several sprites for one character, each with its own animation: walking, jumping and falling, for example.
How to create a sprite

items: Right-click **Sprites** and choose **Create Sprite**.
Give it a name. Start sprite names with `spr`, e.g. `sprPlayer`. Click **Edit Sprite**.
Click the sheet-of-paper icon to make a new image. Leave the width and height at **32** pixels and click OK.
Click the pen to edit the image, and use the magnifying glass (+) to zoom in.
Draw your player with the toolbox. Fill the area: it will look very small on screen!
Click the green tick to confirm, check the preview, then click the green tick again to save.

blocks.text: You then make the other sprites the same way: a square wall (`sprWall`), a bad guy (`sprEnemy`) and a collectible key (`sprKey`). Don't spend ages perfecting them; you can improve them at the end.
Use a **[[naming convention]]**: a short prefix that says what type of resource it is. `spr` for sprites, `obj` for objects, `rm` for rooms. Then `sprPlayer` and `objPlayer` are easy to tell apart.

blocks.title: Key points
items: GameMaker is a 2D game engine that uses drag-and-drop actions.
A sprite is an image (or animated set of sub-images) representing something in the game.
An animated sprite has several sub-images.
Sprites in school are 32 × 32 pixels by default.
Use prefixes like spr, obj and rm to name resources clearly.

pages.spec: Understand objects, instances, events and actions, and use them to make a player move
pages.summary: An object is a template that uses a sprite and has events and actions; an instance is a copy of it placed in a room. Events (like a key press) trigger actions (like Move Fixed).

blocks.text: Objects and instances

To see a sprite in the game or interact with it, you need to make it into an [[object]]. An object can be moved, act on other things and be seen on screen. Not every object needs a sprite: some objects are invisible and just control the game.

The object itself is not placed into the game. It acts as a **template**. An [[instance]] is a copy of the object placed in a room (level). So you could make one tree object and place one hundred instances of it in a room, or one wall object and use 100 instances to build a maze.
Think of a cookie cutter. The cutter is the **object**; every cookie you cut out is an **instance**.
Events and actions

Each object can have several [[event|events]]. An event is something that happens in the game, like a key being pressed, two objects colliding or the object being created. Inside each event you drag in [[action|actions]]: what the object should do when that event happens.

head: Event
Example action
rows: Move Fixed: stop the *other* object (the player)
blocks.caption: Events trigger actions

blocks.text: Making the player move

items: Right-click **Objects → Create Object** and name it `objPlayer`.
Click the icon next to `<no sprite>` and choose `sprPlayer`. Tick **Solid**.
Click **Add Event → Keyboard → Left**.
From the **Move** tab, drag in **Move Fixed** (the red arrows). Click the left arrow and set the speed to **5**. Click OK.
Repeat for Up, Down and Right, then click OK to save.

blocks.title: Worked example: why won't my player stop?
blocks.context: After adding Left, Right, Up and Down events, you test the game. What happens if no key is pressed, and how do you fix it?
steps: The player keeps moving, because nothing tells it to stop.
Open `objPlayer` and choose **Add Event → Keyboard → <No key>**.
Add **Move Fixed**, click the **centre square** (no direction) and set the speed to **0**.
Run the game (green arrow) and press **Esc** to exit.
blocks.answer: With no key event, the player keeps moving. A <No key> event with Move Fixed at speed 0 makes it stop.

blocks.text: Walls and collisions

items: Create `objWall` using `sprWall` and tick **Solid**.
Add **Event → Collision** with `objPlayer`. A [[collision]] event runs when two instances touch.
Add **Move Fixed** set to stop (speed 0), applied to the **Other** object, which is the player.
Put walls around the whole room and some in the middle, then test.

blocks.title: Worked example: the player won't fit through the gap
blocks.context: The player is 32 × 32 pixels and the gaps between walls are also 32 pixels, so the player gets stuck. How do you fix it?
steps: Exit the game with Esc. Double-click `sprPlayer` and click **Edit Sprite**.
Choose **Transform → Scale…**
Set the percentage to **80**, with both **Horizontal** and **Vertical** ticked so the sprite isn't stretched.
Test again, then do the same for `sprEnemy`.
blocks.answer: Scale the sprite to 80% so it is smaller than the gaps.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An object is a template; an instance is a copy of it placed in a room.
One object can have many instances (one tree object, 100 trees).
Events are things that happen (key press, collision, create); actions are what the object does.
Move Fixed with speed 0 stops an object.
Scale a sprite to 80% (both directions) if it won't fit through gaps.

pages.spec: Understand rooms and use them to build levels, a key that moves you on, and a win screen
pages.summary: A room is where you place instances; every game needs at least one. Rooms are used for levels, title screens, help pages and end screens, and a collision with a key can send you to the next room.

blocks.text: Rooms

A [[room]] is the area where you place your objects. You **must** have at least one room for a game to run, but you will usually need many more: one for **each level**, plus rooms for the **opening screen**, **help pages** and **credits/end screens**. The room is the design of what the player sees, so make it aesthetically pleasing (attractive to look at) to make players want to play your game.
Making your first room

items: Create a room, go to the **Settings** tab and give it a meaningful name, e.g. `rmPractise`. You can also add a caption.
Go to the **Objects** tab, select `objPlayer` at the bottom and click in the room to place an instance.
Click the green tick to save.

blocks.text: A key to the next level
In our game, collecting the key takes you to the next level.

items: Create `objKey` with `sprKey` and tick Solid. Place an instance in your room.
Test: the player runs straight over the key, because no event tells the key what to do.
In `objKey`, choose **Add Event → Collision → objPlayer**.
From the **main1** tab, under Rooms, drag **Next Room** into the Actions. You can choose a transition effect too.

blocks.title: Worked example: FATAL ERROR!
blocks.context: You collect the key and the game crashes with a FATAL ERROR. Why, and how do you fix it?
steps: The Next Room action tries to go to the next room in the list.
There is only one room, so there is no next room to go to.
Create a second room called `rmLevelOne`.
Add a player and a key to the new room and save it.
blocks.answer: The error happened because there was no next room. Adding rmLevelOne fixes it.

blocks.text: Score, lives and a win screen
Some objects have **no sprite**, because they only control the game. They appear as a **?** in the room editor because there is no image to show, and they are invisible when you play.

items: **SetScore** object: in its **Create** event, use the Score tab to show the score and lives in the window caption, and **Set Lives** to 3. Place it once in the first room.
**finishGame** object: in its Create event, **Display a Message** ('You Win!'), **Show Highscore**, then **Restart Game**.
Create a room called `YouWin` and place `finishGame` in it. It must be the **last** room.

blocks.text: Rooms run in the order they appear in the list. Any new levels must go **between** the practice room and `YouWin`, or players will win before playing them.
Extensions: add a front page ('Press space to start') and coins. When the player collides with a coin: **Destroy Instance** and **Set Score** to 10, ticking **Relative** so 10 is added to the score.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A room is where instances are placed; every game needs at least one.
Use rooms for levels, title, help and credits screens.
A collision with a key + Next Room moves the player on.
Next Room with no next room causes a fatal error.
Controller objects with no sprite appear as ? in the room editor.

pages.spec: Explain how sound and backgrounds affect a game, and describe the main game genres
pages.summary: Sound (music and SFX) and backgrounds set the mood and must suit the genre and audience. A genre groups games by their challenges and gameplay: action, adventure, RPG, simulation, strategy and sports.

blocks.text: Sound
Sound, also called audio, is an important part of making a game engaging and keeping players interested in the gameplay. There are two main types:

items: **Background music**, which plays throughout a level and sets the mood.
**[[Sound effect|SFX]]** (sound effects), which play when something happens: losing a life, collecting a coin, finishing a level.

blocks.text: Sound can change the mood very quickly. A scream could darken the mood, while a hand-clap could celebrate completing a level. Sounds also tell you whether you are playing successfully, without you having to read anything.
Backgrounds

Like sound, the **background** can drastically change the mood or feeling of a game. A dark background can make a game seem scary; a bright, light background makes it more child-friendly. The background should reflect the game's genre: mismatched elements make a game feel clunky and unsuitable for its target audience.
Genres

A [[genre]] identifies the style or category of a piece of work, like a book, film or poem. Games fall into genres too. Games are not usually grouped by their content (what they're about), but by the **challenges, story and gameplay** they contain.

head: Genre
What it involves
Examples
rows: Physical challenges needing hand–eye coordination and motor skill. The player controls most of the action. Many of the earliest video games were action games. Subgenres include platform, fighting and shooter games (shooters have been one of the dominant genres since the 1990s).

Not defined by story, but by gameplay **without** reflex or action challenges. You solve puzzles by interacting with people or the environment, usually in a non-confrontational way. A 'purist' genre that avoids action beyond mini-games.

You play one or more 'adventurers' who specialise in skills (e.g. melee combat or casting spells) while following a storyline, often travelling an overworld full of monsters to reach towns, dungeons and castles.
Pokémon, The Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy
A diverse super-category designed to closely simulate parts of a real or fictional reality.
The Sims, Microsoft Flight Simulator, Farming Simulator
Careful, skilful thinking and planning to win; the scale ranges from world domination to squad tactics.
Civilization, Age of Empires, chess games
Simulate real sports. Opponents can be real people or artificial intelligence (AI).
EA Sports FC, Rocket League, Mario Kart (racing)

pages.spec: Describe how games are played on consoles and mobiles, and explain VR and AR
pages.summary: Most games are played on consoles, computers or phones, bought in shops, downloaded or by subscription. VR puts you inside a computer-made 3D world with a headset; AR adds computer images onto the real world.

blocks.text: How do we play games?
Think about **what** you use (hardware and software), **where** you are (at home, on the bus to Enniskillen, in an arcade) and **how** you pay.

items: **Game consoles** such as PlayStation and Xbox are the platform for many games. Games may be bought in a shop on a disc and inserted, bought and downloaded online, or played through a **monthly subscription**.

**Mobile gaming** is more and more popular, with games bought or downloaded free from the app stores on phones and tablets. Many are played in a similar way: navigating levels to collect credit and eventually win.
**Computers**: PCs and laptops, with games from online stores.

blocks.text: Newer, less common technologies are emerging and their popularity is increasing rapidly: **VR** and **AR**.
Virtual reality (VR)

[[VR]] stands for **Virtual Reality**. It is a world that doesn't exist: it has been created by a computer and lets users experience and interact with a 3D world using a **VR headset**. The headset shows a 360° view of the computer-generated world, which changes as you turn your head. Extra technology can add sound and movement, such as hand controllers.
Well-known VR games include **Beat Saber** and **Half-Life: Alyx**, played on headsets like the Meta Quest and PlayStation VR.

Older notes call Minecraft 'the most well-known example of VR'. Minecraft is a 3D block-building game in a procedurally generated world (built by the computer as you explore) and is the best-selling video game of all time, with over 300 million copies sold. It has had VR versions on some headsets, but it is normally played on an ordinary screen, so it is not a true example of a VR game.
Augmented reality (AR)

[[AR]] stands for **Augmented Reality**. It means adding computer-generated images on top of real life, usually seen through a phone or tablet camera. For example, some furniture shops have apps that let you see how a sofa would look in your own living room. AR uses the device's **camera** and often its **internet connection** and **GPS**.

The biggest example is **Pokémon Go**, released for Android and iOS devices in **2016**. It uses the phone's GPS to locate, capture, battle and train virtual creatures that appear as if they are in the player's real location. By the end of 2016 it had been downloaded more than **500 million** times. As well as using AR, it encouraged physical activity, and some businesses said it increased profits because more people walked past their shops.

AR
rows: The real world with computer images added
Phone/tablet camera, GPS, or AR glasses

blocks.title: Key points
items: Games are played on consoles, mobiles and computers; bought on disc, downloaded or by subscription.
VR = Virtual Reality: a computer-made 3D world seen through a headset.
AR = Augmented Reality: computer images added on top of the real world.
Pokémon Go (2016) is the best-known AR game, with 500 million downloads in 2016.
Minecraft is the best-selling game ever, but it is not really a VR game.

pages.spec: Explain scoring and target audience, and plan a game with a storyboard
pages.summary: Scores are a way of measuring success, but not every game uses them. Games must suit their target audience. Storyboards plan every screen before you build the game, as in the Magic Amusements brief.

blocks.text: Scoring

[[Scoring]] refers to an abstract quantity (usually **points**) linked to a player or team. Events in the game can raise or lower the score. Most games use score as a measure of success, and in competitive games the goal is often to get a better score than your opponents.

items: Scoring is very different from game to game and is often seen as the 'way to win'.
**Fortnite** and **Apex Legends** have no high score table; they use a **'last man standing'** approach instead.
Some games have **no score at all**, yet you can still win. **Solitaire** (the card game) is a good example: you win by clearing the cards.

blocks.text: Target audience

The [[target audience]] is the particular group of people that a product, such as a film, advert or game, is aimed at. When developing a game, keep the target audience in mind all the time, because they are the people who will play it.
For example, Fortnite is aimed mainly at young teens, while Chess is aimed at logical thinkers and often an older generation of gamer.

blocks.title: Worked example: deciding the target audience
blocks.context: How do you decide who a game is aimed at from a picture of it?
steps: Look at the **colour scheme**: bright, cartoon colours suggest young children; dark, realistic colours suggest teenagers or adults.
Look at the **icons and characters**: cute animals point to young players; soldiers or monsters to older players.
Think about the **gameplay**: simple tapping suits young children; complex strategy or fast reactions suits older players.
Check the **age rating** (PEGI 3, 7, 12, 16 or 18).
blocks.answer: e.g. A bright, cartoon puzzle game with big buttons and a PEGI 3 rating is aimed at young children; a dark, realistic shooter rated PEGI 18 is aimed at adults.

blocks.text: Practical assessment: Magic Amusements

**Magic Amusements** is an up-and-coming game development company in Belfast. It specialises in 3D games, but wants to expand by developing a **2D game aimed at teenagers aged 10–14**, made in GameMaker with a continuous theme throughout and a title suitable for the target audience. The game must have:

items: An introductory **title screen** with a company logo and instructions for reaching the main menu.
A **main menu** that lets the user start the game, access a help feature, view the high scores, load the previously saved game and view the credits.
At least **three levels**, each slightly harder, all possible to complete.
A **scoring system**.
**Collectables**.

blocks.text: Storyboarding

A [[storyboard]] is a set of sketches planning each screen before you build it, labelled with the **colours**, **fonts** and **layout** you will use. For the brief, storyboard your opening/front page, loading screen, each level, help page and final/end credits screen.
Don't skip planning. Building straight away without a storyboard usually means a messy game with no consistent theme.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Scoring is a measure of success, but games like Fortnite use 'last man standing' and Solitaire has no score at all.
The target audience is the group a game is aimed at; colours, characters, gameplay and age rating show it.
The Magic Amusements game is a 2D GameMaker game for ages 10–14.
It needs a title screen, a main menu, three or more levels, scoring and collectables.
Storyboard every screen, labelling colours, fonts and layout.

pages.spec: Know what programming is, who the first programmer was, and why programming skills are useful
pages.summary: Programming (coding) is writing instructions in a language computers understand. Ada Lovelace was the first programmer; there are about 700 languages, and programming builds skills used in many jobs.

blocks.text: What is programming?

[[Programming]] is everything involved in making, controlling and communicating with digital devices. It is often called **coding**, because it involves writing in a language that computers can understand. This lets us develop devices, apps and technology in our own way. A [[programmer]] is a person who writes code for a device and also **tests** the code to make sure it is fully functional (works properly).
The first computer programmer

**[[Ada Lovelace]]** (1815–1852) is famous as the first computer programmer. She worked with **Charles Babbage**, who designed the first general-purpose computer, the **Analytical Engine**. In 1843 Ada wrote what is seen as the first algorithm intended to be carried out by a machine, to calculate a series called the Bernoulli numbers. She also saw that machines could go beyond pure calculation, for example to create music. That is why she is cited as the first computer programmer.

**How many programming languages?** There are roughly **700** programming languages in use today. They exist because different jobs need different features. Some are very good for app development, web development, phone and tablet development, operating system development or general software development. Famous ones include Python, Java, JavaScript and C#.
Jobs in programming

IT jobs have grown considerably every year and are often very well paid. Programming leads directly to jobs such as: It also helps in careers that are not directly in IT: **medicine and dentistry** (analysis skills), the **army** (problem solving), **analyst** roles (analysing everything) and **marketing** (all of the above). Jobs that use programming directly include:

items: Software engineer
Network architect
IT project manager
Database administrator
Web developer
Systems analyst
Mobile app developer
IT consultant
Technical sales rep
Support analyst
Cyber security specialist
Social media manager

blocks.text: **Why learn programming?** Programming lets you give machines instructions, but it also teaches four key thinking skills you will use for the rest of your life:

head: Skill
What it means
rows: Pulling information out of a scenario to understand the problem, so you can create sensible solutions.
Working with ideas (concepts) rather than physical things.
Seeing relationships, and the consequences of actions that haven't happened yet.
Finding solutions to anything, and thinking outside the box (forward thinking).

blocks.text: Programming you already know

In ICT you have used **Scratch** and **BBC micro:bits** (drag-and-drop, event-based programming) and **HTML** web design, where you met a lot of computational thinking. You have also used the three basic programming concepts in other subjects:

head: Concept
Meaning
Where you met it
rows: [[Sequence|Instructions]] in a logical order, one after the other. An algorithm is a sequence of instructions.
The program decides whether a line or group of lines should be run, usually with an IF statement.
Repeating steps using loops: count-controlled, condition-controlled or infinite.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Programming (coding) means writing instructions in a language a computer understands.
A programmer writes and tests code.
Ada Lovelace, who worked with Charles Babbage on the Analytical Engine, was the first programmer.
There are about 700 programming languages, each suited to different jobs.
Programming builds analysis, abstract thinking, pattern recognition and problem-solving skills.
The three basic concepts are sequence, selection and iteration.

pages.spec: Know what C# is, what a compiler does and how Visual Studio (an IDE) helps you write code
pages.summary: C# is a high-level, strongly typed language made by Microsoft. A compiler turns it into binary, and we write it in an IDE such as Visual Studio, starting a Console App project.

blocks.text: C#: a high-level language

At ERGS we learn **[[C#]]** (pronounced 'C sharp'). It was written by Microsoft, is versatile, relatively easy to learn and has lots of documentation. It is used by companies like Microsoft and NASA, and is the main language of the **Unity** game engine, used to build games such as **Pokémon Go** and **Among Us**. The Stack Overflow website was built with ASP.NET, which also uses C#. C# is an object-oriented language that runs on Microsoft's **.NET** framework. You can use it to make Windows applications, websites and web services, mobile apps, video games, AR and VR, and much more.

Computers only understand binary. A [[compiler]] is the program that converts our human-readable code into the binary code the computer understands. This process is called **compiling**. We don't usually write in binary!
A strongly typed language
C# is **[[strongly typed]]**: you must say what type of data each variable holds before you use it. It means writing a bit more code, but has long-term benefits:

items: **Built-in documentation**: you can see how each data type works.
**Increased readability**, helping programmers work in teams.
**IntelliSense**: predictive text for code.
**Help with debugging**: it knows what can and can't happen with a data type before you even run your code.

blocks.text: Visual Studio: an IDE

Programmers don't write code in any old application. Basic packages like Notepad exist, but most use an [[IDE]] (Integrated Development Environment), which brings all the tools for viewing, writing, testing and running code together in one place. We use **Visual Studio**. Its features include:

items: **Line numbering**: tells lines apart in long programs and shows where errors are.
**Colour coding of keywords**, and coloured underlines: a **red underline** shows a syntax error.
**Collapsible code sections**: make large programs easier to view.
**Clipboard**: copy and paste.
Access to objects, methods and properties while you design.

blocks.text: To start: choose **Create a new project**, pick the **Console App** template (make sure it is the **C#** version), enter a project name with no spaces and click **Create**. A [[console]] application uses a text-only window, so we can focus on the fundamentals of C#.

School computers are managed by C2K, which limits what can be coded on them to keep them secure. In Year 10 you can practise in an online tool such as dotnetfiddle.net and Codecademy's *Learn C#* course; at GCSE you use a virtual machine.

blocks.title: Key points
items: C# is a high-level, strongly typed language made by Microsoft; Unity games such as Pokémon Go use it.
High-level languages are close to English; low-level languages are close to binary.
A compiler converts human-readable code into binary.
Strong typing gives documentation, readability, IntelliSense and help with debugging.
An IDE such as Visual Studio has line numbers, colour coding, red error underlines and collapsible code.

pages.spec: Write, run and comment a first C# console program using Console.WriteLine()
pages.summary: Every C# console program has the same structure, starting in the Main method. Console.WriteLine() shows text, every statement ends with a semicolon, and // starts a comment.

blocks.text: The program structure

blocks.title: Program.cs
blocks.output: Hello World!

blocks.text: Think of it like an author writing a series of books:

items: `using System;` says 'we're going to use some premade tools'.
`namespace myFirstProgram` is the name of the **book series**. Its `{` and `}` show where the series starts and ends.
`class Program` is **one book** in the series, with its own `{` and `}`, inside the series.
`static void Main(string[] args)` is a **chapter**. Every program starts in this Main method.
`Console.WriteLine("Hello World!");` is the **first sentence**.

blocks.text: In newer versions of Visual Studio, tick **'Do not use top-level statements'** when making the project, so you see this full structure.

**The magic command.** To make text appear on the screen we use `Console.WriteLine()`. `Console` is the **object**, `WriteLine` is the **method**, the text in speech marks is the **message**, and the `;` is the **line terminator**. Every instruction (statement) must end with a [[semicolon]], like a full stop at the end of a sentence.

To run your program, click the green **Start** (play) button. If there are errors in the **Error List** at the bottom, the program won't run: treat them as clues to a puzzle. For example, 'error CS1002: ; expected' means you are missing a semicolon at the end of the line.

blocks.text: Comments

A [[comment]] is text in a program that the computer ignores. Comments explain what code does, help other people understand it faster, and let you switch off a line to see how the program runs without it. In C#, anything after `//` on a line, or between `/*` and `*/`, is a comment. Visual Studio shows comments in **green**.

blocks.text: The box analogy

A [[variable]] is like a storage box in the computer's memory (RAM). It holds data while the program is running, and it is called a *variable* because the value inside can change. To use a box you need two things:

items: A **name**: the label on the box (the variable name, also called an identifier).
A **[[data type]]**: what kind of thing fits inside the box, e.g. a whole number or text.

blocks.text: In C# you must state the data type **before** you can put anything in the box.

**Data types.** Data types tell the computer how data can be stored, what operations can be done with it, and which methods it can be used with. Without them, a computer might try something impossible, like squaring a piece of text, and that is how we get bugs. C# is also **statically typed**: it checks you used the correct types before the program even runs.

What it holds
Example

rows: Whole numbers (integers), about −2.1 billion to +2.1 billion
Numbers with a decimal point (about 15–16 significant digits, **not** just two decimal places)

blocks.text: Other types you may meet: `long` (bigger whole numbers, 8 bytes), `float` (less precise decimals, 4 bytes), `decimal` (money values, 16 bytes) and `DateTime` (moments in time from 00:00:00 on 1 January 0001 to 23:59:59 on 31 December 9999). You don't need to learn the ranges, but always choose a type of suitable size.

**Declaring and assigning.** To create a variable, write the **data type**, then the **variable name**, then `=` and the **value**, then a semicolon: `int score = 50;`. Creating the variable is called **[[declaration]]**. The `=` is the **assignment operator**: the value on the right is stored in the variable on the left. Note that C# prints a `bool` as `True` or `False` with a capital letter.

blocks.text: Imagine apps that didn't listen to you: no search bars, no login screens, no game controls. Boring! Useful software gathers data from the user and reacts to it. Interactive programs follow a simple flow: **Input → Process → Output**.
Capturing input with Console.ReadLine()
`Console.ReadLine()` pauses the program until the user types some text and presses **Enter**. You store what they typed in a variable: `string name = Console.ReadLine();`
`Console.ReadLine()` **always** returns a `string`, even if the user types a number. If you need to do maths with it, you must convert it.
**Converting data types.** Because C# is strongly typed, sometimes we need to change the type of a value. This is called **[[data type conversion]]**. There are two kinds:

head: Implicit conversion
Explicit conversion
rows: Happens automatically because no data is lost
You must ask for it, because data could be lost
int → double (a double can hold any int)
double → int using the cast operator `(int)`
`9.99` becomes `9` (the decimal part is chopped off, not rounded)

blocks.text: The most common way to convert input is with the `Convert.To…` methods. In `int myValue = Convert.ToInt32("42");` the value "42" is in double quotes, so the computer thinks it is text. `Convert.ToInt32` is a predefined method that turns the string into an integer. (The 32 means it is a 32-bit integer, which is what `int` is.) For decimals, use `Convert.ToDouble()`.

pages.spec: Use the arithmetic operators + - * / and %, and the shortcuts ++ and --
pages.summary: C# uses + - * / for maths and % for the remainder. Dividing two ints gives a whole number; use a double to get decimals. ++ adds 1 and -- takes 1 away.

blocks.text: Arithmetic operators
Programs often need to do calculations. [[Arithmetic operator|Arithmetic operators]] work on numbers (`int` and `double`) to create new values.

blocks.title: Arithmetic.cs

blocks.text: **Watch the data types.** When both numbers are `int`s, the answer is an `int`. 3 doesn't go into 5 evenly, but `5 / 3` still gives the whole number **1** (the remainder is thrown away). In `5 / 3.0`, one number is a `double`, so the answer takes the 'bigger' data type and is a `double`: **1.6666666666666667**.
`7 / 2` is **3**, not 3.5! If you want decimals, make at least one of the numbers a double: `7 / 2.0` = 3.5.
C# follows BIDMAS, just like Maths: `2 + 3 * 4` is 14, but `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.

**Modulus %.** The [[modulus]] operator `%` gives the **remainder** after a division. It uses the percent sign but has nothing to do with percentages. It is useful for checking whether a number 'fits' into another: `17 % 2` is 1, so 17 is **odd**; `18 % 2` is 0, so 18 is **even**.

blocks.text: **Operator shortcuts.** We often need to update a variable, e.g. `apple = apple + 1;`. Programmers love shortcuts, so this can be written `apple++;`. The double plus means **[[increment]]** (increase by 1). `apple--;` **decrements** (decreases by 1). `apple += 5;` adds 5.

pages.summary: A WHILE loop checks a condition and keeps repeating while it is true, so it suits situations where you don't know how many repeats are needed. If the condition never becomes false, you get an infinite loop.

blocks.text: **The WHILE loop.** A `while` loop is best for **indefinite** iteration, where we don't know how many times the code will run, like waiting for a user to enter the correct password. It checks the condition **before** running the code block. If the condition is true, the code runs, then it checks again. It keeps looping **until the condition is false**. It looks a lot like an IF statement, but instead of running once, it repeats. Here `!=` means **not equal to** (≠). In the password program below, we don't know how many times the user will get the password wrong, but the loop repeats until they enter the correct one.

blocks.text: Infinite loops

One of the biggest dangers of a WHILE loop is an [[infinite loop]]. **Explained to a 10-year-old:** it's like getting stuck on a roundabout and never being able to take the exit. It happens when the condition to stop the loop never becomes false, so the computer keeps running the same code forever. Eventually the program can freeze or crash.

A common cause is forgetting to update the variable inside the loop. In the password program, if you left out `myVar = Console.ReadLine();` inside the loop, a wrong password would print 'Try again' forever.
Infinite loops are sometimes useful, for example a traffic light system that must repeat forever:

pages.spec: Understand methods and objects, and plan, build and test a program using the core four skills
pages.summary: Methods are named groups of instructions that run when called, and can take parameters and return answers. Every program is built from the core four: variables, input/output, selection and iteration. Plan, build in small steps, keep code clean and test it.

blocks.text: **Methods.** A [[method]] is a small group of instructions that runs when it is **called** in the code. The code inside runs in sequence, and only when the method is called. `Main` is a method, and so are `Console.WriteLine()` and `Console.ReadLine()`.

items: You call a method using its name followed by brackets: `SayHello();`
If a method accepts an input, the value goes in the brackets. This input is called a **[[parameter]]**. When creating the method, you must state the data type it expects, e.g. `string name`.
A method can send an answer back to where it was called using `return`.

The answer is 11

blocks.text: C# programmers usually start method names with a capital letter (PascalCase), e.g. `SayHello`, and variable names with a small letter (camelCase), e.g. `firstName`.

**Objects and instances.** C# is an **object-oriented** language. Object-oriented programming is based on **[[object (programming)|objects]]**, which each have their own **properties** (attributes, i.e. data) and **methods** (things they can do), and which can interact with one another. Objects let us reuse code written for one object in another without rewriting it all.
You have met this idea in GameMaker: an object is a template and each instance is a copy placed in the game. In C#, a **class** is the template and each object made from it is an instance.

**The core four.** Whether you're designing the next viral game or a secure bank login, it all comes down to four building blocks. Programming is simply giving a computer a set of instructions to solve a problem.

blocks.text: Plan, build, tidy, test

items: **Plan first (flowchart).** Don't touch the keyboard yet! Sketch the flow: what variables do you need, where does the loop start, what condition triggers the IF? Code without a plan becomes 'spaghetti code' that is hard to fix.
**Build iteratively: code, test, repeat.** Declare variables first; get the input working; add the IF statements; wrap the code in a loop **last**, to avoid infinite loops while testing.

**Keep code clean.** Developers spend more time reading code than writing it. Indent code inside curly braces, use meaningful names (`number1`, not `xfgdfgd` or `var1`) and use `//` comments to explain tricky logic.

**Test and review.** Swap with a partner and try to break their program with unexpected input (e.g. letters when it asks for a number). Does the loop end correctly? Are the IF statements logical? Is the code easy to read?
